https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text: Developer Jean Nassif claimed ‘the premier is my best friend’ in a secretly recorded phone call. Photograph: PR IMAGE View image in fullscreen Developer Jean Nassif claimed ‘the premier is my best friend’ in a secretly recorded phone call. Photograph: PR IMAGE Independent Commission Against Corruption Property developer claimed ‘the premier is my best friend’ in tapped phone call, Icac hears Charles Perrottet, the younger brother of the former premier, tells Icac that claims made by Jean Nassif in the call were ‘bravado’ and ‘far-fetched’ Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Penry Buckley Thu 3 Sep 2026 05.14 EDT First published on Thu 3 Sep 2026 02.28 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A property developer who allegedly made prohibited donations to support factional Liberal work claimed “the premier is my best friend” in a secretly recorded phone call the day after Dominic Perrottet was chosen as New South Wales premier, an inquiry has heard. Charles Perrottet, the younger brother of the former premier, told the Independent Commission Against Corruption (Icac) on Thursday that claims made by property developer Jean Nassif in a phone call lawfully intercepted by police were “bravado” and “far-fetched”. Dominic Perrottet is not named as a person of interest in Icac’s allegations and is not accused of any wrongdoing. Nassif, who fled Australia for Lebanon in 2022, has withdrawn from an expected video appearance on Friday after providing a medical certificate. He has previously denied any wrongdoing. As part of its inquiry into alleged corruption in the NSW Liberals, Icac is investigating the allegation that conservative factional figures Charles Perrottet, Jeremy Greenwood and Christian Ellis received prohibited donations totalling $2m from Nassif or his company Toplace between 2020 and 2023 in exchange for political outcomes. The outcomes included damage to the career of former NSW Liberal minister, David Elliott, who had opposed Nassif’s developments, and the removal of former building commissioner, David Chandler, who was scrutinising defects in Toplace apartments. Ellis is overseas and has not responded to Icac’s allegations, while Greenwood will appear before the commission again next week. Charles Perrottet has repeatedly denied he accepted payments from Nassif in exchange for political outcomes. On Thursday, the commission heard phone call between Nassif and a friend in which the developer claimed: “The premier is my best friend … They’re my friends and my boys”. “I only started yesterday. You’re gonna be surprised soon, no jokes, no jokes. I’ve got my hand on the state government, and you’re gonna see changes. You’re gonna see DA approvals for me, like every second week, one DA approved,” he said. Inside knowledge or ‘making stuff up’? Charles Perrottet’s advice to Jean Nassif put under microscope by Icac Read more Charles Perrottet, who described a phone conversation between Nassif and his younger brother Jean-Claude Perrottet, in which the developer claimed he had “forced the boys” to get rid of the Liberal branch of Baulkham Hills in Elliott’s seat as “bravado”, said the October 2021 call was “even more far-fetched”. On Tuesday, the commission heard about a May 2021 meeting between him and Nassif at the Nobu fine-dining restaurant in Melbourne’s Crown Casino. Afterwards, Charles Perrottet wrote he had told the told the developer “the best way to get the building commissioner off his back is to take the fight to Elliott and dismantle his infrastructure”, with the result that Elliott would “be on his knees”. Referencing the Nobu dinner, counsel assisting, Peggy Dwyer SC, suggested on Thursday it was “little wonder … that Jean Nassif thought that he had the right [faction] in his pocket immediately after your brother got the premiership.” “I think it’s just bravado. He says he’s the premier’s best friend,” said Charles Perrottet. The inquiry has previously heard that Charles Perrottet, who texted his wife Anita about a plan to remove Elliott from his ministry once the Perrottet government had formed – writing “ we execute the prick once party room is over ” – shared a secret phone recording in which Elliott could allegedly be heard criticising Dominic Perrottet. On Thursday, the commission heard the recording, during which speaking was faintly audible beneath a loud, rhythmic sound, which Dwyer suggested was a “a heartbeat that suggests a recording device”. Charles Perrottet suggested it was a pocket dial, saying he did not recall having the recording until it was mentioned in evidence last week , or how he had obtained it. The commission heard evidence that he passed it into another NSW Liberal MP and that Ellis shared it with a private investigator employed by Toplace in the hope of improving the audio quality. ‘Charles fucked this whole thing’ Charles Perrottet has previously said he would regularly mislead Nassif, adding a “political flavour” to advice in order to chase up payments for genuine lobbying work by Beckington, a company controlled by Ellis and Greenwood. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion On Thursday, the commission heard an exchange sent by Greenwood to Ellis in April 2020, expressing concern about losing Toplace as a client when Nassif’s Cherrybrook development proposal was refused after the Hills shire council did not support it. Charles Perrottet said he did not know what the message – in which Greenwood wrote “Charles fucked this whole thing” – meant. He was asked about a subsequent exchange between him and Ellis in which he detailed steps to assist with Toplace developments, including a call he wrote he would make to the NSW Liberal MP and former Hills shire councillor Robyn Preston. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email On Thursday, Charles Perrottet said he could not recall calling Preston. The counsel assisting, Peggy Dwyer SC, asked if he would “regularly lie to Christian Ellis at that time to tell him you were doing some things and not others?” “I may have,” said Charles Perrottet, suggesting it might have been “to sound supportive”. Dwyer, noting he had also said he would lie to Nassif, suggested that “actually the fabrication is the evidence you’re giving to the commission because you want to make it sound like you didn’t take the active steps that are clearly set out in this text”. “No,” said Charles Perrottet. Later, he was asked about a message from Greenwood to the Toplace executive Sharangan Maheswaran, also named in Icac’s allegations, in 2021, asking for payment from Nassif, or “Charles is just going to cut the relationship”. After Maheswaran offered to pass on the message, Greenwood expressed concern that Nassif might see it as a threat. Maheswaran, who is named in a separate allegation, has previously denied any wrongdoing. He will appear before Icac next week. Under repeated questioning from Dwyer, Charles Perrottet rejected the suggestion it was “clear as day … that Mr Greenwood shared your view, as expressed to Jean Nassif, that he had to hand over the money in order to achieve the political outcomes”. Icac’s inquiry continues. https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text: Composite: Guardian Design/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Composite: Guardian Design/Getty Images Opinion Sweden How Sweden lost its soul – and stopped being Sweden Martin Gelin In 2022, my country entered a new era of cruelty. It will take more than one election to get the old, tolerant Sweden back Fri 11 Sep 2026 00.00 EDT Last modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 05.14 EDT Share L ast year, a baby named Emanuel was born in Sweden. Before his first birthday, his parents were told that Emanuel could no longer stay in the country. The department of migration ordered his removal, alone, to Iran – despite the ongoing war. Emanuel’s parents were legally in the country. They had Swedish residency permits, but the laws that allowed them to stay were tightened after the baby’s birth, and the family got sucked into a Kafkaesque maze of official hurdles, designed to limit migration to Sweden . Raif is a four-year-old boy with autism, who still wears nappies and is unable to talk. This spring, he was informed that he would be deported alone. Raif’s case attracted significant media coverage and the authorities eventually reversed the decision. But the number of absurd, hardline calls from the migration department just keeps piling up. A 74-year-old British man with dementia was told to leave the country after 25 years. Another British man, on a generous World Bank retirement pension, was also told he was not welcome in Sweden because retirement money does not count as salary for the purposes of new income thresholds for migrants. The young, the old, vulnerable people, the wealthy: all are the target of harsh and often aggressive immigration policies. And Sweden’s leaders remain unyielding. “We cannot adjust the law based on each and every personal fate,” Ulf Kristersson, the prime minister, said, commenting on a series of hardline immigration decisions involving children. View image in fullscreen Election posters of Swedish Prime Minister and Moderate Party leader Ulf Kristersson in Stockholm Photograph: Jonathan Nackstrand/AFP/Getty Images Swedes vote in a general election on Sunday 13 September and, according to opinion polls, the centre-left opposition has a slight lead. But even if there is a change of government, many previously unthinkable far-right ideas are now comfortably embedded in the mainstream of Swedish politics. The past four years have been characterised by an astonishing acceptance of ethnonationalist views, xenophobic rhetoric and authoritarian policies, increasingly targeting children. And many of these ideas have been absorbed and appropriated by the centre-left opposition Social Democrats. Not even the deportation of toddlers or the alarming new shift in judicial policy to build prisons for teenagers as young as 14, are too much of a moral red line, it seems. T he story of the transformation that now blights Sweden goes back to 2022, when the conservative bloc won that year’s Swedish general election, but only with a tiny margin. The Tidö agreement struck that December, between the three conservative parties (Moderates, Christian Democrats and Liberals) and the far-right Sweden Democrats meant a minority government could be formed. But this formal pact breached the mainstream’s cordon sanitaire against cooperating with the radical right. It also launched an attempt to redefine modern Sweden, marking profound policy shifts on immigration, crime, climate and energy, schools and healthcare. Establishment conservatives defended the accord on the grounds that it would blunt the impact of the Sweden Democrats, whose support had been growing since 2015. Instead, it in effect passed the torch of conservative leadership to the far right, giving the Sweden Democrats no ministerial jobs but extraordinary power to shape policy. As a Swede who lived in the US for two decades, I was reluctant to admit that my birth country had changed. I brushed away alarming anecdotes as isolated cases, or a brief departure from the status quo. Surely, Sweden would remain itself, guided by the progressive, egalitarian and humanitarian ideals that defined the country and its public life – at least on the surface – when I was growing up. But in the last four years the Overton window of acceptable debate has shifted radically to the right. A new Sweden has emerged, cruel and cold for migrants, including highly skilled employees of research institutions, universities, tech and medical companies – who have been stunned to learn that they are no longer welcome to work in a country where they have lived for years, sometimes decades. Only 15% of Swedes approve of Donald Trump . And yet ideas quite similar to Trump’s ethnonationalism now define much of contemporary Swedish politics, and are challenging our democratic foundations. The Swedish Institute for Human Rights, an independent government agency, claims that Sweden is increasingly shaped by growing acceptance of xenophobic views, hate crimes and by punitive policies directed at children. In its 2026 annual report it expresses “serious concern” over an erosion of human rights in Sweden. The legal watchdog Civil Rights Defenders also claims that a shift has taken place, where the government no longer talks about rights, but about control. Ministers have entwined migration with crime, and increasingly depict citizens, even children, as problems, risks and costs. If this authoritarian turn can be widely accepted so quickly in Sweden, where the democratic and humanitarian foundations were until recently solid, it can happen anywhere. A string of scandals in the final sprint of the election campaign has not been kind to the far right. Expo, a Swedish magazine that monitors far-right extremism, reported that one of the most influential ideologues in the Sweden Democrats, Gustav Gellerbrant, lives with a partner – who also works for the party – and is alleged to have deep ties to Russian influence operations. Gellerbrant was one of the architects of the Tidö agreement and sits in the Sweden Democrats’ coordinating office within the government. He has been placed on paid leave following the reports but Peter Hultqvist, a Social Democrat former defence minister, called the matter a “security crisis” for Sweden that “goes right into the prime minister’s own office”. Gellerbrant himself was unapologetic, denouncing what he called a media “witch-hunt” – a Trumpian strategy that has also become the new default whenever scandals envelop the Swedish far right. If the rightwing coalition loses the election, it is also prepared to find a scapegoat: Muslim voters. Over the past few months, influential rightwing pundits have lined up to suggest that the left is mobilising Muslims to vote them out. A writer for the newspaper Svenska Dagbladet recently referred elsewhere to a reported increase in early voting in immigrant-majority suburbs as “the cattle” being herded by leftwing parties. In just a few years, conservatives have distanced themselves from their two most recent prime ministers, Fredrik Reinfeldt and Carl Bildt, who advocated a more inclusive, centre-right liberalism. In the government’s “cultural canon ” – originally a strange nationalist initiative promoted by the far right – the authors mock Reinfeldt for his pro-immigration views and blame his “internationalist” agenda for most of Sweden’s contemporary problems. The cultural canon, a list of the references and ideas that supposedly define Swedishness excludes all works from the multicultural Sweden that has emerged since 1975 – meaning we get Ingmar Bergman, Ikea, Pippi Longstocking and the Viggen fighter jet, but nothing made by my generation, the most diverse in Swedish history. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion View image in fullscreen Bibi Andersson and Liv Ullmann in Ingmar Bergman’s 1966 film Persona. Bergman features on the government’s ‘cultural canon’ Photograph: United Artists/Allstar The conservatives have imported the most toxic tropes of the US culture wars in a populist performance of such intensity that it has become internalised on the right, and normalised by the media. Now when a conservative politician in Lidingö, the wealthiest suburb of Stockholm, calls for a ban on “strange Peruvian fish stews” in the school cafeterias, it barely makes the headlines. This embrace of rightwing populism has also led to a departure from Sweden’s ambitious climate politics and a general turn away from scientific consensus. Johan Rockström, a climate scientist, last year told me that he had been invited by every government in Sweden in the past few decades, left or right, to share his research on planetary boundaries , but the current government was the exception – they have not reached out a single time. The government increasingly ignores advisory bodies that are supposed to weigh in on any legislation or proposals. This is most evident when it comes to authoritarian crime policies. New bills have repeatedly been passed against the advice of experts, criminologists and social scientists, who warn against imposing ever-harsher punishments on children. What we are seeing is a fundamental challenge to the Swedish tradition of pragmatism. The small but persistent lead for the opposition in election polls may suggest that the tide is turning, and that there is still an underpinning of humanitarian ideals grounding Swedish voters. Recently, the billionaire Roger Akelius, who used to vote conservative, said he would not vote for the rightwing coalition in this election. “Sweden can’t build a future on isolation and prisons,” he said. View image in fullscreen A row of posters for the Social Democrats, featuring party leader Magdalena Andersson, in Stockholm, September 6, 2026. Photograph: Tom Little/Reuters But the opposition struggles to articulate a clear ideological alternative, preferring a painfully cautious campaign similar to Denmark’s Social Democrats or the UK Labour party as it was under Keir Starmer. There is a clear risk in taking no risks. Relying only on carefully poll-tested centrist positions has not worked for European progressives as the political landscape shifts towards anti-establishment ideas and fury at the status quo. The tight polls suggest that millions of Swedes still consider prisons and isolation the future. Eight years ago, the conservative prime minister Ulf Kristersson promised a Holocaust survivor he would never form a government with the far right. “My values are not those of the Sweden Democrats,” he said in an interview . “I will not cooperate, engage in dialogue, collaborate, or form a coalition government with the Sweden Democrats.” Now Kristersson is promising the far right cabinet positions. The Sweden Democrats have not changed in those years. But Sweden certainly has. Martin Gelin writes for the Swedish newspaper Dagens Nyheter Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? Brussels is steering Europe toward totalitarianism and a “Euro-Gestapo” while lecturing Russia on democracy, Slovak MEP Lubos Blaha has warned. Blaha made the remarks during a European Parliament debate on Tuesday, responding to EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas, who denounced Russia’s recent parliamentary elections as undemocratic. The politician questioned why Brussels was focusing on Russia while cracking down on dissent within the bloc. He cited arrests of pro-Palestinian protesters in Germany and the imprisonment of Estonian opposition figures, who he claimed were jailed for opposing war with Russia. “Are you going to set up the Euro-Gestapo here, Mrs. Kallas, and lock up everyone who wants peace?” he asked. The Slovak lawmaker also questioned why Brussels was debating Russia’s elections while Europe faced mounting unrest. “You may not have noticed, but Spain is in the streets, France is in the streets, and you are here dealing with Russian elections. You must be joking,” he said. Blaha went on to accuse Brussels of double standards over Ukraine’s suspended presidential elections. “You blame the Russians for having elections, but you don’t mind that [Ukraine’s Vladimir] Zelensky has been governing for three years without any elections, without a mandate,” he said. “You are hypocrites!” Zelensky’s presidential term expired in May 2024, but elections have remained suspended under martial law. Blaha also cited the annulment of Romania’s 2024 presidential election, claiming the vote was canceled because “the wrong candidate won.” Romania’s Constitutional Court scrapped the result over alleged irregularities and accusations of Russian interference after EU- and NATO-skeptic Calin Georgescu won the first round. Pro-EU candidate Nicusor Dan won the rerun in May 2025. The MEP argued that Russia had held elections despite the ongoing conflict and daily Ukrainian missile and drone attacks on its territory. The September poll saw the ruling United Russia party win nearly 58% of the party-list vote. Blaha also defended Russian President Vladimir Putin, contrasting his popularity with that of Western European leaders. “You have nothing to criticize Putin for, Mrs. Kallas,” he declared. “Unlike you and your Merzes and Macrons, he has the support of his own population.” Recent polls have put German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s approval rating at a record low of 10% in October, while French President Emmanuel Macron’s support fell to 17% in September. Neither Kallas nor European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen was directly elected to her current position by voters, having assumed office through the EU’s institutional appointment process. Blaha belongs to Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico’s Smer-SD party, which opposes EU sanctions on Russia and has criticized Western military assistance to Ukraine. https://www.rt.com/news/646931-mep-blasts-euro-gestapo-democracy-russia/ PLEASE VISIT: YOURDEMOCRACY.NET RECORDS HISTORY AS IT SHOULD BE — NOT AS THE WESTERN MEDIA WRONGLY REPORTS IT — SINCE 2005. Callous Kallas: The bitter diplomat dragging the EU down the warpath with Russia As bills rise and industry weakens, many Europeans are asking why Brussels keeps prioritizing escalation over diplomacy and daily needs By John Gaffney Kaja Kallas, the Estonian diplomat and former prime minister currently serving as the vice-president of the European Commission, has shown a deeply confrontational attitude towards Russia and the Russians. It is perhaps worth pausing here to note that this is particularly personal, given her family history. Her mother, Kristi Kallas, was only six months old when she, together with her mother and grandmother, was deported to Siberia during the Soviet mass deportations of March 1949. She remained there until she was ten, and later studied medicine and worked as a pediatrician. Her father, Siim Kallas, had a very different experience with the Soviet system. He was a member of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union from 1972 to 1990 and held senior positions in the financial system of Soviet Estonia, including heading the Estonian branch of the USSR Savings Bank. He later became President of the Bank of Estonia, Prime Minister of Estonia and a Vice-President of the European Commission. These two sides of her family history – one marked by deportation and the other by a successful career within the Soviet system – form a striking background to Kaja Kallas’s present-day political position. Last month, Kallas described the German people as being blind to the Russian threat because of their resistance to providing further financial support to Ukraine. Now, I suppose Russian people are also considered blind because of the convincing victory of President Vladimir Putin’s party in September’s legislative election. I am definitely not blind. Kaja Kallas is not alone in her hostility towards Russia. Other senior EU officials, including European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, have supported substantial financial and military assistance to Ukraine. The EU has committed up to €90 billion in support for Ukraine for 2026 and 2027, including funding for both defense and general budgetary needs. The question Europeans should be allowed to ask is how these decisions affect their own societies. Public money is limited, and European citizens also need investment in healthcare, education, transport, housing and infrastructure. Since 2022, Europeans have been paying a heavy price for the transformation of their energy system. The decision to move away from Russian pipeline gas was made in the name of security, and the EU has succeeded in diversifying its supplies. But security has come at a considerable economic cost. The European Commission reports that although wholesale energy prices have fallen substantially from the extraordinary peaks of 2022, industrial gas and electricity prices remain two to four times higher than in the EU’s main trading partners. The Commission warns that this continues to threaten the long-term competitiveness of European industry. The EU’s energy import bill reached €604 billion in 2022 before falling to €427 billion in 2024. Meanwhile, industrial energy prices remain considerably above their pre-crisis levels. Germany, the industrial heart of Europe, has felt the consequences particularly sharply. German industrial energy consumption fell by 9.1% in 2022 and another 7.8% in 2023, with the German Federal Statistical Office explicitly linking these declines, particularly in energy-intensive industries, to significantly higher energy prices and associated production reductions. Germany’s broader economic performance tells the same story. Its economy contracted for a second consecutive year in 2024, while manufacturing gross value added fell by 3%. The Federal Statistical Office identified high energy costs, together with stronger international competition and other structural pressures, among the factors weighing on the economy. Manufacturing remained under pressure in 2025, when value added in the sector fell another 1.3%. Europe faces an uncomfortable question: Is it prepared to accept permanently higher energy costs while production and investment increasingly move towards countries where energy and manufacturing costs are lower? It is one thing to pursue energy security; it is another to allow the foundations of European industry to become the price of achieving it. The issue of NATO and Ukraine is equally contentious. The argument that NATO expansion towards Ukraine ruined Moscow’s relations with Europe is not just a Kremlin talking point – reputable Western analysts, like Professor Jeffrey Sachs, have repeatedly argued the same point. Even if that analysis remains disputed, it is an argument that deserves to be heard in any serious discussion of the origins and continuation of the war, which continues to have devastating consequences for Ukrainians. European leaders should be asking what policies can bring the conflict closer to a negotiated settlement rather than simply allowing the confrontation to continue indefinitely. Perhaps the most revealing part of this story is that the argument is no longer simply between the EU and its critics. It has begun to unfold within Europe itself. Defense spending in the EU is rising at an extraordinary pace. According to the Council of the EU, member states spent €418 billion on defense in 2025, and expenditure is estimated to reach €454 billion in 2026 – 75.3% higher than in 2021. Defense investment alone is projected to reach almost €163 billion in 2026. But the question of who decides how this enormous effort should be organized is becoming increasingly contentious. In September, Kaja Kallas withdrew plans for a new high-level advisory group on European defense after several member states objected. Reporting by Defense News and Euractiv identified Germany, France and Italy among the governments pushing back against the initiative. The German position was that NATO remains the primary framework for military capability and defense planning. The disagreement was not about whether Europe needs defense. It was about who should set priorities, how decisions should be coordinated, and whether another Brussels structure was the right way forward. Even as European governments prepare to spend hundreds of billions more on defense, there is no agreement about the political direction those resources should serve. The EU, in other words, is having two conversations at once: how much it should spend, and what kind of Europe that spending is meant to create. Ms. Kallas, Europe needs diplomacy as well as security policy. European citizens need their governments to protect their interests, use public money responsibly and keep open the possibility of a peaceful future. If the EU continues indefinitely along the present path, the economic and political consequences for European societies will deserve much greater public discussion. EU citizens have the right to ask difficult questions about how their money is being spent and what kind of Europe they want to build. They may disagree strongly about Russia, Ukraine and NATO, but that does not make their questions illegitimate. I was born in Ireland and have been affiliated with Russia for thirty years. I have been living here for the last eight years. From that perspective, I believe Europeans should be able to discuss these issues without being dismissed as blind, naïve or sympathetic to one side simply because they question current policies. Europe has enormous resources and enormous human potential. With wiser choices about priorities, Europeans should be able to expect excellent healthcare, education, transport and infrastructure alongside a responsible security policy. https://www.rt.com/news/646947-callous-kallas-warpath-russia/ READ FROM TOP. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckpd.text: Image source, Bloomberg via Getty Images By Imogen James Published 10 minutes ago Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, says it has covered 90% of the $6.3bn (Â£4.7bn) assets stolen in a hack on Thursday. The remaining 10% may take longer to source in the required amounts, the company added. Binance has consistently pledged to cover 100% of the losses from what is suspected to be crypto's biggest hack on record and said it has set aside more than $6.34bn in company funds to do so. "Binance will absorb the financial impact of these stolen funds, not our users," the company said in a statement on Saturday. It said it had replenished the assets using various funds and its own corporate treasury. All holdings of the cryptocurrencies bitcoin, ethereum and Tether are covered, along with seven other widely-traded crypto assets, the company said. From Bitcoin to Binance: Crypto terms and what they mean The company said its next goal is resuming withdrawal services for users, saying it remained on track to reopen withdrawals on Sunday 1 November and would provide a further update once details were confirmed. The hack is believed to be the largest in history, eclipsing the record of a $1.5bn heist on the Bybit exchange in 2025. Binance's initial investigation suggested an engineer's laptop was compromised, which allowed access to unauthorised withdrawals, but a later update said they had uncovered "additional points of breach". Richard Teng, Binance's co-chief executive officer, said the hack was carried out by more than one person, and the hackers used sophisticated methods to hide their tracks, such as a "self-destruct mechanism". On Friday, the company said it had frozen around $3bn of stolen assets after working with law enforcement, intelligence firms and partners. The investigation is ongoing, it added. The US Secret Service said on Friday it is "working around the clock" with private sector partners "to identify, freeze, trace, and recover funds" stolen from Binance. Two major blockchain analytics firms say they have robust intelligence pointing to a North Korean state-backed group called The Lazarus Group, also known as TraderTraitor, as the likely culprits. The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) said North Korea was responsible for the theft of $1.5bn on the Bybit exchange last year. North Korea has always denied involvement in these attacks. Binance, founded in China in 2017, lets users buy, sell and trade digital assets - it is estimated to have hundreds of millions of users worldwide. Crypto is a digital asset, which doesn't exist physically and is instead accessed via digital wallets or computers.
